title: Tall Timber Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Tall Timber wells have a 225 ft median depth; see local yields, water levels, risks, and estimated drilling costs.
intro_html:
Buying land in Tall Timber means buying into mountain-bedrock conditions, not a predictable shallow aquifer. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a median completed depth of 225 feet, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 49 feet below the ground surface.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, where water can be concentrated along fractures and change substantially from one property to the next. Check nearby permits, the well construction record, and the permit requirements before committing to a purchase.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Tall Timber?
sections.html:
Depths vary widely in this mountain setting. The middle half of reported wells runs from 45 to 400 feet, while the median is 225 feet. About 31% are under 100 feet, 29% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 32% are between 300 and 600 feet. Another 9% reach 600 feet or more; the deepest record is 1,402 feet.

For a drilling bid, that spread matters more than the median alone. A nearby shallow well does not prove the same fracture system exists under your lot. Use wells in Tall Timber and nearby Seven Hills, Mountain Meadows, Crisman, Pine Brook Hill, Sugarloaf, and Sunshine as local evidence, not as a promised depth.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Tall Timber well make?
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household uses, but the well’s storage, pressure system, and permitted use still matter. A pumping test and the actual well report are more useful than a regional average.

Reported results are mixed: 70% produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, 18% are in the 1 to 5 gallon-per-minute range, and 3% are under 1 gallon per minute. That low-yield group is a real buying risk. Ask how the test was performed and whether the result represents sustained production rather than a short-term recovery rate.

sections.heading: What do Tall Timber water levels show?
sections.html:
Among the 145 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 49 feet, with the middle half from 11 to 100 feet below the surface. This is the water standing in the well when it is not being pumped, not necessarily the depth where the producing fracture begins.

The decade medians are uneven: 29 feet in the 1960s, 41 in the 1970s, 40 in the 1980s, 6 in the 2000s, and 80 in both the 2010s and 2020s. The more recent records show deeper reported water levels, but the small subset and changing locations do not prove a region-wide dropping water table.

sections.heading: Who has drilled here, and how active is the area?
sections.html:
The permit history shows long-term development around Tall Timber. Records include 65 permits from the 1950s, 186 from the 1960s, 876 from the 1970s, 580 from the 1980s, 656 from the 1990s, 406 from the 2000s, 305 from the 2010s, and 235 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

In the records, the most active listed drillers are Ground Water Systems Inc. (Wilson, Richard R.) with 829 wells, Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 467, and Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.) with 274. Those counts describe permit records, not a recommendation or proof that a company is currently available.

sections.heading: What does it cost to drill a well in Tall Timber?
sections.html:
Fractured granite and gneiss make drilling cost sensitive to depth and ground conditions. The local model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 225-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $14,600 to $22,500.

A finished household well costs more than the hole. Including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, the model puts a median-depth finished well at about $20,600 to $34,500. Treat that as a planning range, not a fixed bid. A deeper-than-expected hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, water treatment, and site-specific electrical or trenching work can change the final price. Get a written scope tied to the proposed depth and equipment.

sections.heading: What risks should a Tall Timber buyer check?
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main physical uncertainties in fractured bedrock. The records include wells under 1 gallon per minute, and depth ranges from shallow wells to a recorded 1,402 feet. Before closing, obtain the permit, construction report, pump test, static water level, and water-quality results for the property and the closest comparable wells.

Environmental history also deserves a site-specific review. Within about 10 miles are 80 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 779 historic mine features, and 68 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not automatically mean a property is contaminated. Test the well water, check septic setbacks and soil conditions, and confirm that the lot has enough room for a compliant septic system, driveway, building site, and replacement area.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Tall Timber lot
sections.html:
Start with Colorado DWR records and compare several nearby wells rather than relying on one favorable result. The local permit mix is primarily domestic or household use at 77%, and 4,210 wells name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. There are only 70 permits naming Alluvial and 36 naming Quaternary Alluvium, with 0% in Denver Basin aquifers. Confirm the proposed well’s allowed use, especially if the property will have more than ordinary household demand.

For a new build, price access, drilling, pump equipment, electrical service, trenching, septic design, and water testing together. An exempt household-use well may be subject to Colorado’s 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, while an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan. Have the driller and a water-rights professional review the permit before construction begins.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Tall Timber, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Tall Timber, the median reported well depth is 225 feet. The middle half runs from 45 to 400 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 1,402 feet. About 32% fall between 300 and 600 feet, so a buyer should budget for substantial variation rather than assume the median depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Tall Timber?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 225-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $14,600 to $22,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,600 to $34,500. A contractor should confirm the scope after reviewing access, geology, and the proposed well location.

faq.q: How much water does a well produce in Tall Timber?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 70%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Still, 3% report under 1 gallon per minute. Request the actual pump test and ask about storage and recovery before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Tall Timber?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles are 80 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 779 historic mine features, and 68 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the property well tested by a qualified laboratory, then discuss any results with a water-treatment professional before occupancy.

faq.q: Are Tall Timber wells drilled into the Denver Basin aquifer?
faq.a: No recorded wells in this area are identified as Denver Basin aquifer wells. The records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 4,210 wells, with 70 naming Alluvial and 36 naming Quaternary Alluvium. That fractured-bedrock setting can vary sharply between lots, so nearby well records are useful but cannot guarantee depth or yield.
